zuylen1981_svihla.citation: Svihla, George (1967) The yeast cell: What did Leeuwenhoek see? The Microscope, 15, 289-300.
zuylen1981_svihla.summary_by_zuylen: Svihla ground and polished lenses similar to Leeuwenhoek's on an electrically driven spindle with modern abrasives, polished on pitch. Some aspherical surfaces by hand-lens exam, but observations do not suggest less than normal spherical aberration. Empirically controlled illuminating NA by source extent; candle efficient for transparent objects. NO numeric resolving power (µm) for Svihla's replicas is quoted by Zuylen.
zuylen1981_svihla.full_text_of_svihla_1967: NOT FOUND this round (Crossref/EuropePMC/curl searches; The Microscope 15:289-300 not open-accessed).

facts: Utrecht 266x instrument: measured resolving power 1.35 µm
Working aperture NA 0.37 (object-side 0.55 mm, eye-side 0.70 mm apertures)
Diffraction-limited theoretical resolve ~1.0 µm at that NA
Walther: spherical aberration prime harmful effect; balance magnification vs resolving power by careful aperture proportional to power, up to ~x270
Craftsmanship and careful aperture control, not secret aspheric technique, made the difference (neutron tomography shows ball-shaped lens)
Of Leeuwenhoek's surviving lenses, nine measured by van Zuylen early 1980s; resolving power range 1.16 to 4 microns.
DIY ball-lens Leeuwenhoek-type replica ~100x initially; later higher claimed screen magnifications. No calibrated µm resolving-power measurement reported.
Replica/simple microscope images: fine hairs <2 µm; hyphae 0.7 µm breadth clearly resolved with 0.7 mm aperture lens
Thanks list includes Dr George Svihla (no Svihla 1967 resolution numbers)
Modern conventional resolution ~0.2 µm; Leeuwenhoek instruments less than 4x less efficient (qualitative comparison)
Modern commercial/hobby replicas (e.g. Chris Kirby) exist; article describes construction, not measured resolving power in µm.
